item.content:encoded: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Fires Char New Guinea Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks. “Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.” According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research. On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades. Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region , went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea’s National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service’s data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures , water shortages , and school disruptions . In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island. “We’re seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia,” said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier.” Over the past two decades , land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017. Sumatra’s fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. “Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets,” said Field. “It’s in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we’re generally seeing the most fire.” Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November. item.title: Philippine government suspends top tech official for alleged misconduct
item.description: The Philippines government’s Ombudsman has suspended a senior Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) official over allegations he assigned government contracts to a company he founded and continued to hold a stake in. The Ombudsman announced the suspension yesterday and named Undersecretary for E-Government David L. Almirol as the individual of concern, after considering “administrative complaints of Grave Misconduct, Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service and violation of … the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.” “In ordering the preventive suspension, the Ombudsman found strong evidence supporting the administrative charges against Almirol,” according to its announcement of the suspension. Almirol founded a company called Multisys Technologies Corporation that offers software development services, plus packaged products. After over a decade as the company’s CEO, Almirol in 2022 joined DICT at the request of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., to work on improving e-government services. The Ombudsman alleged that between 2023 and 2025 DICT awarded at least eight contracts valued at over ₱1.5 billion ($24 million) to entities linked with Multisys. The contracts covered information and communications technology consultancy, e-government application deployment, web-based messaging services, cloud infrastructure, data center colocation and software subscriptions. Evidence of those transactions is apparently on the record in Multisys’s books. Local laws mean Almirol should have divested his stake in Multisys within 60 days. The Ombudsman alleges the exec missed that deadline but later complied. It’s not alleged he issued contracts in the period during which he continued to hold Multisys shares. The Ombudsman has suspended Almirol without pay for six months, a step it says is necessary because if he continued in the role it “could prejudice the investigation, particularly given his control and custody of documents and evidence relevant to the case.” The org has also pointed out that its decision does not pre-judge the matter, but is “a precautionary measure intended to preserve the integrity of the proceedings and ensure an impartial and unimpeded investigation.” President Marcos Jr. made rooting out corruption a key plank of his platform and even created an agency to tackle the problem. However, it’s felt that some anti-corruption actions may have been partly politically motivated. Past tech-related scandals in the Philippines include a 2022 case that saw its Department of Education overpay for lousy laptops . ®

item.title: To help world gorge on GPUs, Nvidia brings cash bucket to fatten wafer-thin supply chain
item.description: Nvidia has decided that its future prospects rest on an improved silicon substrate and packing supply chain, so has dipped into its giant pile of cash to ensure it can get the parts it needs by ensuring its suppliers have the resources needed to play their small part in keeping the flow of GPUs and AI processors strong. It’s not unusual for manufacturers to invest in their suppliers, because it helps to create certainty and spread financial risk. For those deals to be announced at a major tech company’s conference – as Nvidia did at its Berlin GTC gabfest – is somewhat novel, suggesting the company feels the need to show investors it is working to ensure it can meet demand for its products, and that demand will persist for years. Several of Nvidia’s announcements pertained to silicon substrates, aka wafers. Whatever you call them, they’re blank, round, silicon slabs onto which chipmakers etch circuits. They’re made by companies that sell to foundries like TSMC and Intel, which then turn them into chips of various flavours. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that demand for AI hardware is vast, but that “Capacity is the constraint.” Specifically, capacity for activities like building substrates, advanced silicon packaging, testing, and creating optical connectors. Big Green therefore plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. To make that happen, Nvidia has added Samsung’s Electro-Mechanics business unit to its substrate supply chain. Samsung apparently has immediate capacity at a factory in South Korea and Nvidia intends to tap that now. The deal means that by 2028, about a quarter of Sammy’s substrate output will go to Nvidia. Nvidia already has a deal with Japanese substrate outfit IBIDEN. In Berlin, the GPU giant pointed to further expansion that will triple production at an IBIDEN plant. Taiwanese substrate player Unimicron is also benefiting from Nvidia’s generosity, in the form of a capacity reservation agreement and associated plant expansion plans. It’s not just wafers that Nvidia wants to tuck into. The company has also signed a capacity reservation with Korean silicon packaging player Amkor. Again, Big Green’s involvement will see its partner expand capacity, in this case by 300 percent. Nvidia says this deal “will support higher production volumes for current and next-generation platforms.” AI systems need speedy networks, and many players see optical connections as the best way to build systems capable of handling the data deluges modern workloads create and require. Nvidia has therefore hatched a plan to boost manufacturing capacity at optics outfit SPIL. Again, Big Green already has a deal with the company, but in Berlin it expanded that arrangement in the hope it expands production capacity 15x by mid-2027, then doubles that again by the end of 2028. All of which suggests that Nvidia believes the AI infrastructure boom has years left to run. ®
item.dc:creator: Simon Sharwood
item.content:encoded: Nvidia has decided that its future prospects rest on an improved silicon substrate and packing supply chain, so has dipped into its giant pile of cash to ensure it can get the parts it needs by ensuring its suppliers have the resources needed to play their small part in keeping the flow of GPUs and AI processors strong. It’s not unusual for manufacturers to invest in their suppliers, because it helps to create certainty and spread financial risk. For those deals to be announced at a major tech company’s conference – as Nvidia did at its Berlin GTC gabfest – is somewhat novel, suggesting the company feels the need to show investors it is working to ensure it can meet demand for its products, and that demand will persist for years. Several of Nvidia’s announcements pertained to silicon substrates, aka wafers. Whatever you call them, they’re blank, round, silicon slabs onto which chipmakers etch circuits. They’re made by companies that sell to foundries like TSMC and Intel, which then turn them into chips of various flavours. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that demand for AI hardware is vast, but that “Capacity is the constraint.” Specifically, capacity for activities like building substrates, advanced silicon packaging, testing, and creating optical connectors. Big Green therefore plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. To make that happen, Nvidia has added Samsung’s Electro-Mechanics business unit to its substrate supply chain. Samsung apparently has immediate capacity at a factory in South Korea and Nvidia intends to tap that now. The deal means that by 2028, about a quarter of Sammy’s substrate output will go to Nvidia. Nvidia already has a deal with Japanese substrate outfit IBIDEN. In Berlin, the GPU giant pointed to further expansion that will triple production at an IBIDEN plant. Taiwanese substrate player Unimicron is also benefiting from Nvidia’s generosity, in the form of a capacity reservation agreement and associated plant expansion plans. It’s not just wafers that Nvidia wants to tuck into. The company has also signed a capacity reservation with Korean silicon packaging player Amkor. Again, Big Green’s involvement will see its partner expand capacity, in this case by 300 percent. Nvidia says this deal “will support higher production volumes for current and next-generation platforms.” AI systems need speedy networks, and many players see optical connections as the best way to build systems capable of handling the data deluges modern workloads create and require. Nvidia has therefore hatched a plan to boost manufacturing capacity at optics outfit SPIL. Again, Big Green already has a deal with the company, but in Berlin it expanded that arrangement in the hope it expands production capacity 15x by mid-2027, then doubles that again by the end of 2028. All of which suggests that Nvidia believes the AI infrastructure boom has years left to run. ®

item.title: PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk
item.description: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something was coming in PHP” on Friday from one of the researchers that found the bugs, Lorenc told us. Later that night, using his company’s AI harness and a frontier model, the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. All it took was a “basic prompt of ‘find bad vulnerabilities in PHP,’” Lorenc wrote in a subsequent LinkedIn post. On Saturday, Chainguard began working with the PHP maintainers, confirmed that some of its findings matched the bug reports, and helped test the patches. “The patches are crazy - this is not a simple vulnerability,” Lorenc told The Register . “It really did take them months to build a real, working patch for it. And then on Monday, the rumors started, and yesterday it just spiraled.” Some people published POCs on social media, other security vendors reported seeing real-world exploitation, and late Tuesday night Lorenc told us he decided to ship the fixes, and notified the PHP coordinated disclosure channel about his plans. “People were getting hit in advance” of the official PHP disclosure, “so we made the call to ship the fixes under that,” Lorenc said. “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild.” Also on Tuesday night, Chainguard published built artifacts and made them accessible to anyone, not just customers. “And then I woke up this morning and saw that this was all our fault,” Lorenc said. When asked if he would do anything differently, given the fallout from Chainguard’s early disclosure, Lorenc said no. “This process and policy is based on trying to coordinate as much as possible until shit hits the fan and people start weaponizing things,” he said. “It sucks, because we really are all on one team, and there's bad guys over there doing stuff.” Chainguard’s honeypots trapped IPs from China and Russia targeting the vulnerabilities on Wednesday, Lorenc added. “Just being told there's a vulnerability in a piece of software - even something as big as PHP - is enough to find it,” he told us. “I did that myself without any other knowledge on Friday." "I think this is kind of the new normal. People are able to build an exploit in hours without even knowing what the vulnerability is." What we know about the CVEs and how to exploit them While we still don’t know the scope of exploitation - or what will happen to vulnerable legacy systems that don’t have security fixes - threat hunters predict it’s going to be a doozy. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them,” Wiz researchers Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld, and Tomer Schwartz warned on Wednesday, adding the oft-quoted stat that PHP powers 70 percent of all websites in the world. “Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4,” the Wiz kids wrote. “Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.” Both bugs are related to how PHP handles memory management and error handling, and both lead to remote code execution (RCE). They can cause a corrupted internal PHP state when a request ends unexpectedly, and then a later request can reuse that state, leading to memory disclosure or RCE. “Both are memory corruption vulnerabilities,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity explained. “If an attacker can shape the memory PHP trusts, they can potentially hijack what it does next, and in these cases that means remote code execution.” CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ) leads to RCE via out-of-memory corruption. “If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory,” the project maintainer wrote. “On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.” CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ) allows RCE via stale state. “A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request,” according to the PGP Foundation. “A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.”®

item.title: ‘It doesn’t look good’: Arteta concerned as Saka limps off against Bayern Munich
item.description: ‘A player off with really sharp pain is never good news’ Winger forced off 10 minutes into Arsenal’s 2-2 draw Mikel Arteta made no attempt to conceal his concern over the quad injury that forced Bukayo Saka out of Arsenal’s 2-2 Champions League draw at Bayern Munich , saying it did not “look good at all”. The manager was delighted with the fight that his players showed, Declan Rice earning a deserved point with an 82nd-minute equaliser. Arsenal had led through Eberechi Eze, who came on in the 10th minute for the stricken Saka, before Harry Kane took centre stage. The Bayern striker set up Alphonso Davies for 1-1 before giving his team the lead from the penalty spot. Continue reading...

item.title: FCC chair warns media not to run the "fake polls" Trump keeps complaining about
item.description: Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing "fake polls," amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media. Carr's post on X said, "Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis... Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." Carr urged broadcasters to "provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered." In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very "context" that Carr said is needed. Read full article Comments

item.title: Broda Shaggi Reveals He Was Hit by a Stray Bullet in New Documentary
item.description: Samuel Animashaun Perry (Broda Shaggi) explains the stray bullet incident behind his months-long hiatus in a new video. If you are a fan of Broda Shaggi ‘s skits, his music, or even just his lively presence on your timelines, you must have noticed that the popular entertainer and actor has been noticeably absent from social media over the past few months. Samuel Animashaun Perry has now officially returned, bringing along a deeply moving mini-documentary that breaks his silence and reveals the terrifying life-threatening ordeal behind his sudden hiatus . The multi-AMVCA winner revealed that his unexpected break was caused by a horrific incident where he was struck by a stray bullet while returning from a shoot. Recounting the frightening moment, Broda Shaggi shared,”We were done shooting and were on our way when we got stuck in a holdup. Suddenly, I heard a loud bang and everywhere went silent. I could see people talking, but I couldn’t hear anything. Then I touched my hip and saw blood. That was when it dawned on me that I had been hit by a stray bullet.” Broda Shaggi in an eccentric futuristic costume for one of his signature video skits. The incident led to an emergency hospital admission, extensive medical procedures, and an intensive period of physical rehabilitation . For a performer whose entire craft relies on boundless physical energy, comedy, and stage presence, being bedridden and unable to move presented immense physical and emotional hurdles . In the video, he candidly reflects on the overwhelming fear of losing his mobility and the uncertainty of how he would continue doing what he loves . Tracing his road from severe setback to resurgence, the documentary shows his gradual process of learning to walk again, moving from complete immobility to crutches and eventually regaining his strength . Now stepping back in front of the camera on his own terms, Broda Shaggi is turning what could have been a tragic end into a triumphant second chapter, ready to reconnect with his fans and dive back into his creative work . Watch below The post Broda Shaggi Reveals He Was Hit by a Stray Bullet in New Documentary appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Xbox wants you to pay 24 to 40 cents per hour to stream games you already bought
item.description: In September, when Microsoft severely limited the game-streaming buffet available to Game Pass subscribers , the company said non-subscribers would soon be able to "purchase cloud playtime hours through the Xbox Store and stream eligible games they own on supported devices." Today, Microsoft rolled out those a la carte Cloud Playtime purchases to Xbox Insiders, with prices that might be a bit galling for players who have already purchased these streamable games. The "introductory launch pricing" for Xbox's Cloud Playtime purchases is as follows: 10 hours for $4 (~$0.40/hour) 25 hours for $8 (~$0.32/hour) 50 hours for $12 (~$0.24/hour) Purchased playtime "remains available until it’s used," Microsoft writes, so you don't have to worry about your 50-hour purchase expiring before you can use it fully. Read full article Comments

item.title: Enterprises keep buying software upgrades that IT thinks will make things worse
item.description: Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms' IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “ The Software Tax .” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide , conducted the survey. Read full article Comments

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
item.description: null On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . (Image credit: NASA) India did not stop at the moon with Chandrayaan-1. In 2019, the country launched the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which carried the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. item.title: Tesla profits drop 43% in Q3
item.description: Tesla published its third-quarter 2026 financial results this afternoon. Earlier in October, it reported its sales and deliveries for the three-month period, selling fewer cars than in the same quarter in 2025 , yet it still beat analyst projections. Now we can see how those sales translate to the bottom line. Tesla brought in $28 billion in revenue in Q3, almost the same as in 2025. Automotive revenues were $20.6 billion, a 3 percent decrease year over year. Perhaps more troubling is the decline in revenue from solar panels and storage batteries—this line of business had been growing, but for Q3 revenue fell 16 percent year over year to $2.9 billion. Services and other revenues, though, which include parts and Supercharger use, grew by a third to $4.6 billion. But the company—like the rest of us—has seen its expenses go up. Operating expenses rose by 39 percent to $4.8 billion, dropping the company’s operating margin to just 2.6 percent; in Q3 2025, Tesla’s margin was 5.8 percent. Net profit fell to $787 million, down 43 percent year over year. What’s more, capital expenditures were up by 110 percent to $4.7 billion, and free cash flow was down 62 percent to $1.5 billion. Read full article Comments

item.title: Barkley and Buendía on target as Aston Villa sink Viking to maintain perfect start
item.description: For a little over 20 minutes, Aston Villa could look down on the rest of Europe. They had scaled the Champions League summit on goal difference when Henrik Heggheim put through his own net and the fact was not lost on the Holte End, who reflected their position in song and perhaps allowed themselves another glimpse back to the days when their supremacy was undisputed. “We’ve conquered before, we’re prepared for more,” the pre-match tifo display had read. Perhaps Villa really will rekindle the spirit of 1982 but the frustration here, albeit minor in the wider scheme, was that they could not maintain their bird’s-eye view over the continent. A superbly taken volley by Peter Christiansen, awarded by the video assistant referee after initially being disallowed for offside, gave Viking a consolation their second-half display deserved and meant Unai Emery’s side must make do with slumming it just behind Paris Saint-Germain. Continue reading...

item.title: Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video
item.description: Olamide releases his new single Burukutu alongside his upcoming album Time & Space. Photo Credit: Olamide/Instagram When the YBNL Nation boss decides to drop new music, the entire continent pauses to listen. Olamide is back in his absolute element, and the music community is buzzing following a major surprise release that has everyone talking. Building on the momentum of his previous self-titled album Olamidé released last year, the rap icon has dropped a brand-new single while officially setting the timeline for his next massive project. Olamide’s latest single is titled “ Burukutu ”. Named after the traditional, locally brewed fermented grain beverage found across various parts of Nigeria, the track leans heavily into street-level jubilation and celebratory culture, opening with the infectious chant, “Baddoo we wanna partyyyy!” Lyrically, Olamide weaves sharp street-smart Yoruba flows with rhythmic cadences, reflecting on hustle, leisure, and local vibes over high-energy production. Olamide holding a saxophone on the courtyard set of his Burukutu music video. Photo Credit: Styling The Stars With Swazzi/Instagram The accompanying music video directed by TG Omori matches the song’s intense cultural weight visually. It cuts dynamically between a monochromatic, glowing red corridor—where Olamide appears sharply tailored in a double-breasted suit, dark sunglasses, and dreadlocks—and an earthen-toned, arched outdoor courtyard filled with rhythmic background dancers in structured white outfits, pillbox hats, and pearl details, alongside striking scenes of Olamide stepping up to play the saxophone. Alongside the release of “Burukutu,” Olamide surprised fans by announcing the official title of his forthcoming studio project: Time & Space. Marking another milestone in his legendary discography, Time & Space is officially scheduled to drop on November 16, 2026, proving yet again why the icon remains at the very heartbeat of African music. Watch the video below The post Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit. The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch. While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability. Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission. All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions. Learn More About Artemis

item.title: OpenClaw creator says he spent $10 million in tokens last month
item.description: Peter Steinberger, member of technical staff at OpenAI and the creator of OpenClaw, estimates that he spent around $10 million in tokens running AI workloads last month. But don't feel bad for him, because it's all coming out of investors' pockets. He made this admission at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, in a conversation with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. He made this admission at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, in a conversation with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. Even if risks like prompt injection have been reduced through engineering efforts, Steinberger said, "you might not want to give your agent all the permissions." Instead, he suggested using an agent to authorize your agent. "You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent," he said. "Many times the agents are like, 'oh yeah, actually maybe I shouldn't do this,' or 'there's a simpler way that keeps it within the guardrails.' So those those two systems combined greatly increase my trust that I just can let the agent rip." ®

item.title: Reach new heights of laziness by burning tokens to let an AI tap your smartphone screen for you
item.description: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable , a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening

If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening the clock app and switching to the stopwatch tab takes it about 96 seconds, which is supposed to be impressive, apparently, as the company behind Opposable decided to showcase it on the thing’s website. As for Opposable’s ability to actually accomplish tasks, well, that’s not exactly a sure thing. “On eight tasks the model had never been tuned on, run on the emulator twice each, giving it the whole task succeeded 4 and 3 times,” the blog post notes. I’m pretty sure my brain and hands can do better without burning tokens to fail. “Giving it one subgoal at a time and checking each claimed success against the accessibility tree before the next subgoal succeeded 6 times in both rounds,” the blog continues - so even when it gets babysat each step of the way, it still only succeeds at three-quarters of tasks. Cool - that’s really going to free up all that time wasted setting timers and doing other mundane tasks on my handset. Why someone would install this on their Android device - which requires sideloading an APK and manually granting access to read and interact with the screen through accessibility settings - seems like a bit of a mystery. Opposable’s website even warns that it could be a security disaster: “whoever holds the token can operate the phone, so treat it like a password,” but still invites users to try. An argument could be made for using Opposable as an accessibility tool for people with difficulty using a smartphone, but this isn’t mentioned anywhere on its website. Opposable is instead billed as a way to “hand off the phone chores,” leaving users free to do something else - just not on the phone currently being slowly controlled by a clumsy AI. Sure, you could give your AI some virtual thumbs through Opposable, but … why? We reached out to the Opposable team to get an answer to that question, but didn’t hear back. ® UPDATED AT 03:25 UTC, OCTOBER 2026 to add that Opposable does not consider its product an accessibility tool. "We do not market it as an assistive tool, because we have not built it or tested it as one," a spokesperson told The Reg by email. "If people with disabilities find it useful, we want to hear from them and build for them." The spokesperson also explained why demos are so slow: "It shows our small model on the Android emulator, on a laptop CPU, with no help from the phone's hardware." When running on phone, Opposable apparently does rather better. However the outfit admits it has done only very limited testing, but is about to do more.

item.title: The new human-crafted Apple Music brand matters in an AI world
item.description: Apple just revealed a new brand identity for Apple Music, with the expected turn to Liquid Glass. I’m not much of a fan of their new design language in general; this is where I admit that I’m still running MacOS Sequoia and have grumpy things to say about rounded corner radii and text legibility. It’s just a trend, it will pass, and at some point I’ll probably cave and upgrade when it starts actually affecting my ability to get work done, or more importantly get security updates. Once I adjust, I’ll stop noticing it, and life will go on. As such, I wouldn’t normally find an obvious rebrand like this notable, much less feel like I had much to say about it. But then I happened to catch Apple’s behind-the-scenes video in my YouTube recommendations, and I realized I did have thoughts. Read full article Comments

item.title: Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee
item.description: Osas Ighodaro standing in her custom thermal-mapped blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee. If these photos of Osas Ighodaro have you staring at your screen a little longer than usual, we completely understand. Because how do you look at a dress this beautiful and simply scroll past? The colours, the design, the way it sits on her body! There’s so much to admire, and we’re right there with you. The Nigerian-American actor, host and producer has given us many reasons to love her fashion choices over the years, but this particular look has us especially curious about how it was made. Dressed in a gorgeous blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee, Osas looks like she stepped straight out of an art exhibition. And once you hear the inspiration behind the dress, you might appreciate it even more. Actor and host Osas Ighodaro wearing a blue mosaic gown crafted from hand-painted mother-of-pearl by House of Marvee. Here’s where it gets interesting. House of Marvee drew inspiration from thermal mapping, using different shades of blue to follow the natural curves of the body. The floor-length gown features hand-painted mother-of-pearl details, creating a mosaic effect that moves between deep ocean blues and brighter turquoise tones. Look closely, and you’ll notice how the colours and textures work together across the fabric. Osas Ighodaro posing in an asymmetrical one-shoulder blue mosaic dress featuring hand-painted mother-of-pearl tiles by House of Marvee. We also love how the one-shoulder design gives the dress room to shine. One arm is covered in a long sleeve, while the other shoulder is left bare, creating a lovely contrast. Osas keeps her accessories simple with gold hoop earrings, allowing the beautiful details of the gown to remain the focus. Osas Ighodaro posing in a House of Marvee hand-painted mother-of-pearl blue gown with gold hoop earrings and a finge And can we talk about her beauty look for a second? The retro finger waves, warm-toned makeup and gold hoop earrings complement those gorgeous shades of blue beautifully. From the hand-painted details to the way the gown follows her silhouette, House of Marvee has given us a dress we’d happily spend a few more minutes admiring. Osas Ighodaro lying down in a custom House of Marvee floor-length blue mosaic dress inside an art gallery space *** Photo Credit: House of Marvee/Instagram The post Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: People are vibe coding copyrighted apps with AI – will tech firms sue?
item.description: AI lets us remake software as we like Dmytro Olegovich Zakharchuk / Alamy Stock Photo I am waging a silent rebellion against Amazon. The internet giant owns Goodreads, the leading service for tracking and cataloguing books, but is generally considered to be a poor steward of the platform, which is built on ageing technology. Frustrated with the user experience, I have used AI to vibe code my own Goodreads app, relegating the official one to mere plumbing in my private fiefdom. Take that, Amazon, for I have breached your terms of service! I am not alone in my AI-enabled rebellion. It feels like I come across daily examples of people using AI to unofficially remix and remake software, whether that is creating a free copycat version of Adobe Photoshop , stripping the ads from their smart TV , mashing up video games or getting printers working on unsupported devices . It is all happening so quickly that lawyers don’t seem to have sprung into action to prevent it, though in some of the more egregious copyright-infringing cases, I would expect them to eventually. Read more Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality For my Goodreads app, Amazon probably doesn’t know, or even care, about what I am doing. I won’t bore you with the full technical details, but I have built the app in such a way that it avoids mass “scraping” Goodreads – systematically harvesting data from its website – which would be easy to detect and block. By treading lightly, my app aims to resemble a human user and fly under the radar. Advertisement This connects to another ongoing battle over the interaction between AI-enabled individuals and companies: AI agents. The promise of an AI agent is that it can go out on to the internet and do things for you, like shopping or booking appointments. A flurry of examples has launched recently, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, and companies have begun fighting back, with the likes of Amazon and JPMorgan Chase blocking Muse in high-profile pushbacks. Ironically, Meta sits on both sides of this battle: its automated tools blocked a protest account on Instagram after detecting activity from a Claude AI tool that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems”. All of this comes down to a much older conundrum: where do your rights end and others’ begin? We have seen this play out every time a major new technology has hit the internet, and the results of a few historical examples might inform what happens next with AI. The first is a technology you probably don’t even think about anymore: your web browser. In the late 1990s, the two main browsers were Microsoft’s Internet Explorer and Netscape’s Navigator. They worked slightly differently, and websites often instructed users to choose one over the other. item.dc:creator: Jacob Aron
item.content:encoded: AI lets us remake software as we like Dmytro Olegovich Zakharchuk / Alamy Stock Photo I am waging a silent rebellion against Amazon. The internet giant owns Goodreads, the leading service for tracking and cataloguing books, but is generally considered to be a poor steward of the platform, which is built on ageing technology. Frustrated with the user experience, I have used AI to vibe code my own Goodreads app, relegating the official one to mere plumbing in my private fiefdom. Take that, Amazon, for I have breached your terms of service! I am not alone in my AI-enabled rebellion. It feels like I come across daily examples of people using AI to unofficially remix and remake software, whether that is creating a free copycat version of Adobe Photoshop , stripping the ads from their smart TV , mashing up video games or getting printers working on unsupported devices . It is all happening so quickly that lawyers don’t seem to have sprung into action to prevent it, though in some of the more egregious copyright-infringing cases, I would expect them to eventually. Read more Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality For my Goodreads app, Amazon probably doesn’t know, or even care, about what I am doing. I won’t bore you with the full technical details, but I have built the app in such a way that it avoids mass “scraping” Goodreads – systematically harvesting data from its website – which would be easy to detect and block. By treading lightly, my app aims to resemble a human user and fly under the radar. Advertisement This connects to another ongoing battle over the interaction between AI-enabled individuals and companies: AI agents. The promise of an AI agent is that it can go out on to the internet and do things for you, like shopping or booking appointments. A flurry of examples has launched recently, including Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots, and companies have begun fighting back, with the likes of Amazon and JPMorgan Chase blocking Muse in high-profile pushbacks. Ironically, Meta sits on both sides of this battle: its automated tools blocked a protest account on Instagram after detecting activity from a Claude AI tool that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems”. All of this comes down to a much older conundrum: where do your rights end and others’ begin? We have seen this play out every time a major new technology has hit the internet, and the results of a few historical examples might inform what happens next with AI. The first is a technology you probably don’t even think about anymore: your web browser. In the late 1990s, the two main browsers were Microsoft’s Internet Explorer and Netscape’s Navigator. They worked slightly differently, and websites often instructed users to choose one over the other. As more browsers flourished, Microsoft pushed back, most notably in 2003 by blocking a competitor browser called Opera from accessing its MSN website, a popular destination at the time. In the end, browsers began misidentifying themselves to websites as other browsers in an effort to avoid this. Today, the right to use any browser you like has essentially won out against the right of websites to restrict them, although the rise of dedicated smartphone apps has put some of the power back in companies’ hands. Nested within this battle was another: ad blockers. Once your browser has fetched the HTML code for a website, should you be obligated to display it all on your screen? As websites began displaying adverts to make money, people began downloading ad blocker add-ons to take back control of their browser. In response, companies developed new techniques for displaying ads, and ad blockers adjusted to remove them. Today there is a stalemate, with around 30 per cent of internet users blocking ads . Finally, there is the grandfather of all internet copyright battles: Napster, a peer-to-peer file-sharing service that people used to illegally share music files . The companies mostly won this battle thanks to the rise of Spotify and other similar music streaming services – with an easy legal option, piracy faded away, the side effect being that most people generally don’t own the music they listen to anymore. Internet users largely prevailed after the browser wars, ad blocking is at an impasse and streaming music seems to have benefitted the big corporations. What does all of this mean for AI? The difference here is decentralisation: just as I have used AI to create my own Goodreads app, so could anyone else, each of them slightly different. Fully blocking them all without restricting normal human access would be a monumental task. There is a slight caveat here – most AI use is centralised through the big providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, and Amazon could theoretically ask them to build in a block against creating such software (or sue them), but I think that is unlikely. In any case, the availability of open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run on their own hardware makes that a losing battle. I think it is most likely that we will be heading for a mix of all three. When it comes to remixing software, anything you do in the privacy of your own computer is going to be very hard to stop. Once you release it online, however, expect the lawyers to hunt you down. What we might see is the sharing of prompts that will get an AI to do the work for you in private – writing “recreate Photoshop, make no mistakes” isn’t something that any lawyer can stop – and there already exists a slightly more complicated version of this in the form of an instruction set for AI called Reverse Engineer Anything . As with browsers, individual choice will win, but this time the choices will be even more granular. Read more Hannah Fry: ‘AI can do some superhuman things – but so can forklifts’ For software that goes out into the wider internet, including AI agents, there will be two tiers. I expect Meta and Amazon will eventually come to some kind of agreement that allows Muse to shop for you. We are already seeing this with the development of a “personal agent protocol” that Meta is developing with businesses, including payment-processing services like Shopify and Stripe . For anyone using a commercial AI agent, what you can and can’t do will be decided by the companies, just as music streaming services dictate how you listen. But why should you use a commercial AI agent? People like me with a little technical know-how and even less coding ability are already using AI to create their own independent agents. As AI gets better at writing software, the barrier to entry will get lower and lower. I think companies will just have to come to accept this, as they have done with ad blockers. In future, a decent percentage of users that look like humans will actually be custom-made bots in disguise, doing things solely for the benefit of their creator. These bots will be ungovernable, for good and for ill. Further AI reading Anthropic has used its Claude AI model to solve a historical cryptography mystery . In the 1990s, the US National Security Agency (NSA) chose five specific mathematical objects called elliptic curves to serve as the basis for a cryptography standard used to generate digital signatures, now known as ECDSA. No one knew how these curves were chosen, but cryptography lore suggests that an NSA employee used a specific phrase , perhaps “Jerry deserves a raise”, to generate them. In fact, Claude was able to guess the specific mechanism – random number generation based on a timestamp – and regenerate the curves. The finding has no implications for cybersecurity, it merely answers a long-running question. Spotify says it has removed 50 million AI “slop and spam” tracks from recommendations on the platform, as part of a range of efforts to put “human artistry first”, according to the firm’s announcement. item.title: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades
item.description: The legendary studio behind series like Mass Effect , Dragon Age , Neverwinter Nights , and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is no more. BioWare announced via social media Wednesday afternoon that "after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending." The official announcement was posted mere minutes after a Bloomberg report detailed 400 job cuts across BioWare parent company Electronic Arts, including 50 at BioWare, based on reports from "a person familiar with the company's plans." "Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," EA executives wrote in a message to staff, according to Bloomberg. Read full article Comments

item.title: Nvidia woos wary Europeans with more open weights models
item.description: Nvidia hopes to capitalize on European sovereign AI demand by unloading a slew of new open weights models spanning chatbots, healthcare, and robotics. The major model devs have the resources to build highly capable models from scratch. But most enterprises don't, and have instead been forced to fine tune open weights models from the likes of Mistral or H Company using their own datasets. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia unveiled its latest additions to its open weights model library with refreshed Nemotron Retriever embedding and Alpamayo autonomous vehicle models. The point of embedding models While by no means the sexiest subclass of models out there, embedding models are some of the more useful ones for enterprise apps. Retrieval augmented generation (RAG), a technology we've explored extensively in the past, relies heavily on the embeddings generated by these models for applications like AI-augmented search. At a high level, RAG works by cutting up documentation in chunks, then converting those into vectors called embeddings. The embeddings are then ranked based on their relevance to the user's query before they're fed into an LLM's context. Nvidia's latest embedding and reranking models, based on Nemotron 3.5, support embeddings of both images and text across 34 languages. This time around, the models are being offered in sizes ranging from one to eight billion parameters, with NVFP4-quantized versions for those running on new Blackwell-based accelerators. That's small enough to run on something like a DGX Spark with plenty of room to spare for other models. Always take vendor claims with the usual grain of salt, but among competing embedding models, Nvidia boasts that at BF16-precision, its new 8 billion parameter embedding and reranking models are now the top-ranked dense models on the ViDoRe V3.1 benchmarks. However, not all documents are easily converted into embeddings. PDFs are notoriously difficult for embedding models to make sense of. They're often scanned from printed source material and formatted for consumption, which means scraping text and parsing charts. For this, Nvidia has also launched a refreshed Nemotron Parse model that's been trained specifically to extract information from PDF documents. Nvidia claims the model can process roughly 10.5 pages a second when running the one billion-parameter model on a single H100. Alongside the new embedding models, Nvidia is also rolling out access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, a more compact version of its autonomous driving model based on which promises real-time processing of streaming video and sensor data when running on the company's DRIVE AGX Thor platform. The models come just a week after the GPU giant launched its Nemotron 3.5 Super vision language (VL) model and teased Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 74 billion-parameter mixture of experts (MoE) model designed to fit in as little as 24 GB of video memory. That model, Nvidia says, will be available for download starting Friday. While open models provide ente

Nvidia claims the model can process roughly 10.5 pages a second when running the one billion-parameter model on a single H100. Alongside the new embedding models, Nvidia is also rolling out access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, a more compact version of its autonomous driving model based on which promises real-time processing of streaming video and sensor data when running on the company's DRIVE AGX Thor platform. The models come just a week after the GPU giant launched its Nemotron 3.5 Super vision language (VL) model and teased Nemotron 3.5 Bolt, a 74 billion-parameter mixture of experts (MoE) model designed to fit in as little as 24 GB of video memory. That model, Nvidia says, will be available for download starting Friday. While open models provide enterprises and governments a path toward sovereign AI, Nvidia's models are somewhat unique in how they're released. Most open weights models are a sort of black box. Anyone can download them, but the data and processes used to arrive at those weights is a mystery. This isn't the case with many of Nvidia's models: Alongside their weights, Nvidia routinely releases the training data and the recipes used to turn it into the final model. This means customers can not only inspect the model at a low level, but build a fully custom model based on Nvidia's Nemotron architecture, rather than trying to modify the weights after the fact through fine tuning. We should note that Nvidia is not the only one to do this. The Allen Institute has employed a similar strategy with its OLMo models for this very reason. ®

item.title: OpenAI's latest AI models are coming to Google Cloud and Antigravity
item.description: Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you'll have more options. OpenAI and Google have come to an arrangement that will see the former's frontier models arrive in Google Cloud services. Perhaps more importantly, GPT models will soon appear in Antigravity, Google's agent-powered coding tool. For enterprise customers and AI enthusiasts, OpenAI's latest model will appear in Google's "Model Garden" in the coming weeks, adding to its 200-plus options. The garden already offers access to Google's Gemini models, as well as an assortment of open models like Mistral, Llama, and Gemma. Anthropic's Claude AI has also been available for some time. Google says it's now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs. While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud. Astra will naturally cost the most to run, but Google's system supports dynamically moving workloads between LLMs based on performance, latency, and efficiency. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA JPL Looks to Next 90 Years of Innovation, Exploration
item.description: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Clockwise from top: Caltech graduate students and friends carry out their first rocket firing on Halloween, 1936, in a dry riverbed along which JPL would rise. Their work helped make possible missions such as Perseverance and Europa Clipper as well as the future SkyFall and MoonFall missions. NASA/JPL-Caltech Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come. Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth. The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7 . It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones. More firsts are on the way. “Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.” Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall , a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans. Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks
