item.content:encoded: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Clockwise from top: Caltech graduate students and friends carry out their first rocket firing on Halloween, 1936, in a dry riverbed along which JPL would rise. Their work helped make possible missions such as Perseverance and Europa Clipper as well as the future SkyFall and MoonFall missions. NASA/JPL-Caltech Interstellar probes. Lunar drones. Helicopters on Mars. When a group of Caltech graduate students and enthusiasts began conducting rocket-propulsion tests in Pasadena’s Arroyo Seco on Oct. 31, 1936, they had no idea that their work marked the inception of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Ninety years later, the lab, now managed by Caltech for NASA, isn’t only celebrating the long line of historic firsts accomplished here; it’s paving the way for many to come. Initially a contractor for the U.S. Army, JPL launched America’s first satellite, Explorer 1 in 1958. But rather than just orbiting Earth like the Soviet Union’s Sputnik, Explorer 1 became the first spacecraft to conduct science, thanks to an onboard Geiger counter that discovered the protective radiation belts encircling Earth. The lab joined part of the newly formed NASA that same year. Within six years, in 1964, JPL sent the first U.S. mission to the Moon, Ranger 7 . It also went on to lead the first planetary flyby, the first probe to visit all four gas giants, the first infrared telescope, the first rovers to roll on Mars, and the first rotorcraft to fly there, among many other historic milestones. More firsts are on the way. “Over the course of 90 years, JPL’s first-of-a-kind missions have transformed our understanding of the universe and our place in it,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL’s director since 2025. In 1992, only a couple years after he started as an engineer at the lab, Gallagher led the JPL team that built and tested the Wide-Field and Planetary 2 Camera for NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, which delivered many of the mission’s most iconic images. “We stand on an extraordinary foundation, and we’re ready to push the boundaries with exciting new missions so that future generations can go even further.” Aiming for a 2028 launch, the JPL-managed SkyFall mission will deploy three helicopters mid-descent over Mars to search to map hidden ice deposits and analyze weather patterns. Helping advance NASA’s Moon Base, JPL is developing MoonFall , a mission that will land a group of large propulsive drones at the lunar South Pole that same year. Set for a 2027 launch, SunRISE (Sun Radio Interferometer Space Experiment) features six toaster-oven-size satellites that will fly in formation to create a miles-wide radio antenna dish in order to study the Sun’s activity. What it reveals could help make space exploration safer for humans. Protecting humanity is also the goal of the asteroid-hunting NEO Surveyor (Near-Earth Object Surveyor) mission, which, managed by JPL, will hunt for potentially hazardous space rocks that other telescopes can’t find. Once an object is spotted, NASA can offer a threat assessment and plan accordingly. Closer to home, the same lab that launched the first oceanographic satellite in 1978 is at work on several missions that will offer a deeper reading of Earth’s vital signs. Where one mission will monitor the movement of water by measuring slight changes in gravity, another will study how powerful tropical convective storms form. A third will detail how different types of air pollution affect human health. They add to a fleet of other Earth missions and projects JPL helps lead, including NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) a joint mission with the Indian Space Research Organisation that can pinpoint how Earth’s surface changes in relation to natural disasters. Another, one of a series of instruments called AVIRIS (Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer), can even detect rare Earth elements critical to modern technology. Flown on airplanes, the AVIRIS sensors were developed at JPL’s Microdevices Laboratory , which invented the “camera on a chip” technology that enables cellphones to take pictures. It’s also where the detectors are being developed for PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), a newly announced NASA mission that will strengthen humanity’s understanding of the universe by studying radiant energy visible only in the far-infrared. “Bringing together the very best of scientific brilliance and engineering ingenuity from across Caltech and JPL continues to advance NASA’s priorities and empower America’s space leadership,” said Caltech’s president Ray Jayawardhana, who is also a professor of astronomy. “I can only imagine what those Caltech students experimenting with rockets in a little patch of dry riverbed would think if they could to see what Caltech and JPL have accomplished since, and where we’re headed next. Ninety years later, the same spirit of daring is still opening new frontiers and inspiring humanity.” The 90th anniversary comes just a few weeks before another milestone, when on Nov. 18 Voyager 1 reaches a full light-day — the distance light will travel in 24 hours, which is some 16 billion miles, or 26 billion kilometers — from Earth. Ed Stone led the mission for 50 years, serving as JPL’s director for 10 of them. Stone died in 2024, but the Voyagers are continuing on their journey deeper into interstellar space, a place no other spacecraft have ventured. Turning 50 next year, they rely on NASA’s Deep Space Network (developed by JPL in the Apollo era) to receive commands and send back science data. Stone said that with both Voyagers exploring regions never before visited, “every day is a day of discovery.” The same could be said for JPL. -end- Media contact Matthew Segal Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 818-354-8307 matthew.j.segal@jpl.nasa.gov 2026-073 Share Details Last Updated Oct 21, 2026 Related Terms Jet Propulsion Laboratory Explore More 6 min read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system… Article 1 week ago 4 min read NASA JPL Testing Readies Voyager Technologies Lander for Moon Mission Article 1 week ago 5 min read NASA’s SPHEREx Telescope Sees Menagerie of Brown Dwarfs Article 2 weeks ago Keep Exploring Discover More Topics From NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory Europa Clipper SkyFall NASA’s SkyFall mission to Mars, building on the success of the Ingenuity helicopter, will send a trio of aircraft to… Mars Perseverance Rover The Mars Perseverance rover is the first leg the Mars Sample Return Campaign’s interplanetary relay team. Its job is to…

item.title: LiteLLM supply chain attack hoovers up passwords and secrets
item.description: Unknown crims compromised LiteLLM's release process on Wednesday, distributing a malicious version (1.107.0) containing malware designed to steal cloud and AI credentials and a remote access trojan (RAT) capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines through PyPI and Docker registries. PyPI quarantined the trojanized version of the popular open source AI gateway within hours, and the Docker image (litellm/litellm:1.107.0) was removed from both Docker Hub and GHCR soon after - but anyone who ran the compromised package on any platform should assume their secrets have been stolen. “Check for /tmp/.pc_once_* (the exfil has already fired if this file exists) and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock (the C2 daemon ran or is still running if this file exists),” advised Aikido Security malware hunter Ilyas Makari. “The same applies to anyone who ran the official Docker image litellm/litellm:1.107.0 , or pulled it via the latest , main-latest , or main-stable tags.” The most recent safe version is v1.106.2. While it’s too early to tell the scale of this latest LiteLLM supply chain attack – an earlier LiteLLM compromise in March potentially exposed more than 2,500 organizations and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines worldwide, according to CloudSEK – make sure to take these measures seriously, and check environments for any indicators of compromise. Aikido, Google’s Wiz cloud security biz, and supply-chain security provider Socket have all published extensive threat-hunting and mitigation instructions for LiteLLM users and security teams, so give those a read stat. LiteLLM, developed by BerriAI, provides a common interface for LLM providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini, and receives about 23 million weekly downloads. This means a compromised installation can run alongside LLM provider API keys, cloud identities, and database connection strings - and expose a ton of valuable credentials, secrets, and other sensitive data to whoever uploaded the malicious package. “Teams using 1.107.0 should stop deploying it and investigate environments where Python ran after installation, including proxy containers and CI runners,” Socket researchers said on Wednesday. The malicious version was uploaded at 11:39 UTC, and according to Wiz kids Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy, the payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm , which is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. Miscreants used this repo to inject the three malicious files into the LiteLLM release pipeline. These, according to Makari, include cook.pth , which causes the second file, cook.py , to run automatically every time Python is invoked on the machine, without any additional user action. Meanwhile, cook.py contains the infostealer, and the third file, sitecustomize.py, is the RAT. item.content:encoded: Unknown crims compromised LiteLLM's release process on Wednesday, distributing a malicious version (1.107.0) containing malware designed to steal cloud and AI credentials and a remote access trojan (RAT) capable of executing arbitrary code on infected machines through PyPI and Docker registries. PyPI quarantined the trojanized version of the popular open source AI gateway within hours, and the Docker image (litellm/litellm:1.107.0) was removed from both Docker Hub and GHCR soon after - but anyone who ran the compromised package on any platform should assume their secrets have been stolen. “Check for /tmp/.pc_once_* (the exfil has already fired if this file exists) and /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock (the C2 daemon ran or is still running if this file exists),” advised Aikido Security malware hunter Ilyas Makari. “The same applies to anyone who ran the official Docker image litellm/litellm:1.107.0 , or pulled it via the latest , main-latest , or main-stable tags.” The most recent safe version is v1.106.2. While it’s too early to tell the scale of this latest LiteLLM supply chain attack – an earlier LiteLLM compromise in March potentially exposed more than 2,500 organizations and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines worldwide, according to CloudSEK – make sure to take these measures seriously, and check environments for any indicators of compromise. Aikido, Google’s Wiz cloud security biz, and supply-chain security provider Socket have all published extensive threat-hunting and mitigation instructions for LiteLLM users and security teams, so give those a read stat. LiteLLM, developed by BerriAI, provides a common interface for LLM providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini, and receives about 23 million weekly downloads. This means a compromised installation can run alongside LLM provider API keys, cloud identities, and database connection strings - and expose a ton of valuable credentials, secrets, and other sensitive data to whoever uploaded the malicious package. “Teams using 1.107.0 should stop deploying it and investigate environments where Python ran after installation, including proxy containers and CI runners,” Socket researchers said on Wednesday. The malicious version was uploaded at 11:39 UTC, and according to Wiz kids Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy, the payload originates with malicious commits made on github.com/Berri-AI/litellm , which is a hyphenated variant of the legitimate BerriAI organization. Miscreants used this repo to inject the three malicious files into the LiteLLM release pipeline. These, according to Makari, include cook.pth , which causes the second file, cook.py , to run automatically every time Python is invoked on the machine, without any additional user action. Meanwhile, cook.py contains the infostealer, and the third file, sitecustomize.py, is the RAT. Python also executes the RAT at interpreter startup, and this file spawns a background daemon that polls the attacker's infrastructure every hour for new commands to execute. Upon executing, the infostealer harvests a ton of sensitive data across 16 modules targeting browsers, cloud providers, and AI services, according to Read and McCarthy. It steals browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari, along with AWS credentials from ~/.aws/, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS). It also collects users’ Google Cloud Platform service account keys and application default credentials, along with Microsoft Azure tokens from the CLI cache. And then it also swipes API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers, plus SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history files. The malware then encrypts all of this stolen data using AES-256-CBC, wraps the encryption key with an RSA-4096 public key, and sends the encrypted data via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled domain: http://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck. BerriAI did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries. This is an emerging story, and we will continue to update it as we learn more details.®

item.title: Digital scents could add a new dimension to virtual worlds
item.description: The familiar scent of orange can now be transmitted through the internet Counter/Getty Images Imagine if, in addition to sharing photos of those muffins you just baked, you could share their delicious aroma, too. That’s the promise of an AI-assisted device that can transmit smells over the internet. So far, it works on only a small number of scents, including orange, beer and cake, but its creators hope the system will ultimately recreate more smells. The scent of a pine forest or the aroma of coffee, for example, could then add a new dimension to virtual worlds and long-distance communication. Although it is now routine to communicate sight, sound and even touch sensations electronically, smell is “still a very undeveloped sense”, says Chunyu Yang at the Ohio State University. That’s partly because odours involve complex chemistry. Whereas vision, for example, can be broken down into combinations of red, green and blue pixels, says Yang, there’s no simple building block underlying smell. Any attempt to convert aromas into electronic signals has to recognise combinations of very different molecules. Read more Smell-seeking drone uses moth antenna to follow a scent To solve the problem, Yang and her colleagues built an electronic nose, or “e-nose”, as well as a smell generator, then used machine learning to connect the two. The e-nose consists of arrays of sensors made of metal oxide. When different gaseous components of smells, such as ethanol (from alcoholic drinks) or limonene (found in citrus fruits), bind to the sensors’ surface, this changes their resistance, creating different electrical signals. Advertisement The researchers then trained an AI algorithm to recognise the distinctive signals created by smells from five different foods or beverages: orange, cake, coffee, beer and red wine. Teaching the AI to correctly recognise the smells was “the most challenging part” of the entire study, says Yang, because to generate enough data to train the system, she had to expose the sensors to the various smells hundreds of times. This information was then sent over the internet to a smell generation device that the researchers are calling “Scentronic”. This part of the system involves miniature containers holding liquids laced with each of the five smells. Above each container is an atomiser that vibrates in response to electric signals, forcing the liquid in the container through a cotton filter and releasing fine droplets into the air, creating the appropriate smell, or combination of smells. When she tested the handheld device on 14 volunteers, they correctly identified the smells being transmitted to them 73 per cent of the time, on average. item.dc:creator: Jo Marchant
item.content:encoded: The familiar scent of orange can now be transmitted through the internet Counter/Getty Images Imagine if, in addition to sharing photos of those muffins you just baked, you could share their delicious aroma, too. That’s the promise of an AI-assisted device that can transmit smells over the internet. So far, it works on only a small number of scents, including orange, beer and cake, but its creators hope the system will ultimately recreate more smells. The scent of a pine forest or the aroma of coffee, for example, could then add a new dimension to virtual worlds and long-distance communication. Although it is now routine to communicate sight, sound and even touch sensations electronically, smell is “still a very undeveloped sense”, says Chunyu Yang at the Ohio State University. That’s partly because odours involve complex chemistry. Whereas vision, for example, can be broken down into combinations of red, green and blue pixels, says Yang, there’s no simple building block underlying smell. Any attempt to convert aromas into electronic signals has to recognise combinations of very different molecules. Read more Smell-seeking drone uses moth antenna to follow a scent To solve the problem, Yang and her colleagues built an electronic nose, or “e-nose”, as well as a smell generator, then used machine learning to connect the two. The e-nose consists of arrays of sensors made of metal oxide. When different gaseous components of smells, such as ethanol (from alcoholic drinks) or limonene (found in citrus fruits), bind to the sensors’ surface, this changes their resistance, creating different electrical signals. Advertisement The researchers then trained an AI algorithm to recognise the distinctive signals created by smells from five different foods or beverages: orange, cake, coffee, beer and red wine. Teaching the AI to correctly recognise the smells was “the most challenging part” of the entire study, says Yang, because to generate enough data to train the system, she had to expose the sensors to the various smells hundreds of times. This information was then sent over the internet to a smell generation device that the researchers are calling “Scentronic”. This part of the system involves miniature containers holding liquids laced with each of the five smells. Above each container is an atomiser that vibrates in response to electric signals, forcing the liquid in the container through a cotton filter and releasing fine droplets into the air, creating the appropriate smell, or combination of smells. Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Editor’s Highlights Sign up to newsletter Yang built several different designs including stringing the atomisers onto a necklace and a wristband, and mounting them on a handheld device. When she tested the handheld device on 14 volunteers, they correctly identified the smells being transmitted to them 73 per cent of the time, on average. She also built a prototype that reproduces taste, involving a cup of water with electromagnetic pumps containing flavoured liquid fixed around its edge. “When it receives information from the internet, the corresponding liquid will be dropped into the cup.” Alternative methods to generate smells remotely have been suggested, including heating wax to release particular scents, and even stimulating neurons directly to create the experience of smell. But Yang argues her method is both fast and practical. She now hopes to expand the repertoire of the system, to create more complex aromas. Why honing your sense of smell could keep you sharp as you age A declining ability to detect scents is linked to conditions including Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. But restoring our most neglected sense might not only reduce cognitive decline – studies also show it could even reverse it She suggests the entertainment industry could be first to develop the technology, to create more immersive virtual worlds. But there could also be health applications. For instance, the smell of food transforms the eating experience, so the technology could be adapted to make soldiers’ or astronauts’ rations more palatable. The Scentronic system could also enable doctors to assess distortions in patients’ sense of smell, for example, in post-viral illness or neurodegenerative disease. The Scentronic system is “a great idea” and a step in the right direction, says Marianna Obrist at University College London, although she points out that recognising a smell and then releasing a matching one from a limited library is very different from the ease with which we can transmit sound and vision. “There’s still a long way to go before we can truly record and replay smell experiences.” Journal Reference: Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee9266

item.title: Sci-fi legend Alan Dean Foster on his new futuristic adventure 'Lost On Paradise': 'It's paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up' (interview)
item.description: null Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, " Lost on Paradise ", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week. Foster famously ghost-wrote the first " Star Wars " novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades. In addition to crafting the screen story for " Star Trek: The Motion Picture ," Foster also wrote the novelizations for the first three "Alien" films , Disney's " The Black Hole ," John Carpenter's "The Thing," "The Last Starfighter," "Star Trek," "Transformers," "Terminator: Salvation", and many more. Lost on Paradise by Alan Dean Foster: $19.99 New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems… View Deal The near-future, off-world escapades of "Lost On Paradise" are the latest addition to Foster’s acclaimed bounty of bestselling standalone novels and series, including the popular "Spellsinger" series. "Earth is crowded, polluted, and dismal," states the novel's synopsis. "Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina scrape by on her poorly paying job and what little money he gets selling items scavenged from rich people’s trash. Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina dream of Paradise. A brilliant cover design heralds the arrival of Alan Dean Foster's latest novel (Image credit: Blackstone Publishing) "Paradise: a beautiful, clean, verdant world where three races live in harmony—at least, according to the videos sent back to Earth. There are the Eiquan, masters of astonishing technology; the Lusanata, hunters and farmers; and humans, who may be restricted to a few scattered settlements, but still live a life ten times better than those on Earth. "On the run after a criminal act, Jonos and Liina finally escape to Paradise. It's everything they hoped for. Until tragedy strikes." The genesis of Foster's "Lost on Paradise" is something that’s been percolating in his fertile mind for many years. "I had this notion of a planet called Paradise where everything is perfect, and everything on Earth is seriously messed up," Foster tells Space. "There’s this couple who have problems; they’re poor like everybody else. "And you have a unique male protagonist because he recognizes that his female partner is smarter than him, so she’s the brains of the outfit, and he supplies the muscle. Although he's not stupid. item.dc:creator: Jeff Spry
item.content:encoded: null Few names in the science fiction literary world carry as much weight and respect as author Alan Dean Foster. His award-winning 55-year career as a grandmaster of the genre continues with his latest novel from Blackstone Publishing, " Lost on Paradise ", and we have an exclusive excerpt to share with our readers ahead of its release this week. Foster famously ghost-wrote the first " Star Wars " novelization for George Lucas in 1976 and "Splinter of the Mind’s Eye" in 1978, which was intended to be a low-budget Star Wars sequel should the space opera not become a hit. He’s been a mainstay for go-to fantastic adventures featuring engaging characters, dynamic plotlines, and imaginative worlds for six decades. In addition to crafting the screen story for " Star Trek: The Motion Picture ," Foster also wrote the novelizations for the first three "Alien" films , Disney's " The Black Hole ," John Carpenter's "The Thing," "The Last Starfighter," "Star Trek," "Transformers," "Terminator: Salvation", and many more. Lost on Paradise by Alan Dean Foster: $19.99 New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems… View Deal The near-future, off-world escapades of "Lost On Paradise" are the latest addition to Foster’s acclaimed bounty of bestselling standalone novels and series, including the popular "Spellsinger" series. "Earth is crowded, polluted, and dismal," states the novel's synopsis. "Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina scrape by on her poorly paying job and what little money he gets selling items scavenged from rich people’s trash. Like millions of others, Jonos and Liina dream of Paradise. A brilliant cover design heralds the arrival of Alan Dean Foster's latest novel (Image credit: Blackstone Publishing) "Paradise: a beautiful, clean, verdant world where three races live in harmony—at least, according to the videos sent back to Earth. There are the Eiquan, masters of astonishing technology; the Lusanata, hunters and farmers; and humans, who may be restricted to a few scattered settlements, but still live a life ten times better than those on Earth. "On the run after a criminal act, Jonos and Liina finally escape to Paradise. It's everything they hoped for. Until tragedy strikes." The genesis of Foster's "Lost on Paradise" is something that’s been percolating in his fertile mind for many years. "I had this notion of a planet called Paradise where everything is perfect, and everything on Earth is seriously messed up," Foster tells Space. "There’s this couple who have problems; they’re poor like everybody else. "And you have a unique male protagonist because he recognizes that his female partner is smarter than him, so she’s the brains of the outfit, and he supplies the muscle. Although he's not stupid. Too often you get a big, hulking guy with no brains. But she has a potentially fatal disease, and they’re trying to get away like a lot of poor people in the world today. So here's a place called Paradise. How do you get there? It’s expensive and difficult. And what happens if they do? Maybe Paradise isn’t always Paradise." "Lost On Paradise" lands on Oct. 20, 2026 from Blackstone Publishing (Image credit: Blackstone Publishing) In crafting a deteriorating New York some 150 years or so down the calendar, it was important to stay sharp regarding developments that pop up in the news to avoid any internal logic conflicts. "You just don’t want to get caught out by a scientific development that you postulate is near future when it's actually contemporary," explains Foster. "So I was very careful with that. But as you’re building out an alien environment and one that’s supposed to be perfect and beautiful, and then there’s maybe some things about it that aren’t, what do you introduce to show that? "You don’t want to contradict yourself when you’re worldbuilding. That's a large problem that’s unfortunately common in science fiction," notes Foster. "Where somebody is breathing air, and suddenly they’re breathing methane, and it just doesn’t work. There’s a lot of different variables that come together that prove that Paradise is Paradise in some ways and not in others. A good example would be when the first Europeans reached Tahiti. The problem was that the people who entered this Paradise brought venereal disease and smallpox, to which the Polynesians had no resistance. So it's Paradise until you get there, and then maybe you mess it up." Now enjoy our exclusive chapter excerpt from Alan Dean Foster’s "Lost On Paradise." Published by Blackstone Publishing. Why shouldn’t a man and a woman in his and Liina’s position try to get to Paradise? Jonos mused as he treaded his way homeward. Though morning continued its ascent, the sun did not. Or so it seemed, when the omnipresent pollution often rendered day as dark as night. The gloom was useful for masking scavenging activities and for concealing one’s identity. It was less suitable for more plebian activities such as breathing and eating. Or living. Life on Earth sucked. But on Paradise… To emigrant humans it went without saying that Paradise was aptly named. Everyone had heard the stories. On Paradise a person could breathe freely. Without a mask, without fear of needing lung implants, without having to worry about inhaling a soupçon of strychnine or similar industrial pollutants. On Paradise food was plentiful and fresh, water devoid of contaminants. There was work, too, for anyone willing to adapt to entirely new surroundings, for those willing to acknowledge the much-talked-about overlordship of the dominant species. For arrivals willing to submit to the experimental, ever-evolving social structure, and to the limitations that were placed on newcomers, the technologically superior Eiquans professed an indifference that amounted to a willing welcome. Or so the compendium of hugely diverse anecdotes insisted. That’s all they were, Jonos knew. Stories and speculation, rumors and conjecture. Ignoring the spotty rain that had begun to fall, he turned a corner and nearly ran over a couple who scrambled to get out of his way. The man he had accidentally jostled started to say something, quickly realized the size of the individual he was about to chastise, and mumbled on his way, dragging a woman—likely his wife—with him. Jonos paid them no mind. Half of him was engaged in navigating his way home, the other half in dreaming of what Paradise might actually be like. In truth, he had never met anyone who had actually been to Paradise. He had never met anyone who knew anyone who had been to Paradise. That did not make the distant world any less real. The media periodically released vits and images of the place. These showed an Earth-like planet swathed in an atmosphere perfectly suitable for humans. The indigenous wildlife was fascinating, the few but thriving, improvised communities intriguing, and the rarely seen Eiquans themselves tall, gracile, and sophisticated. So what if they weren’t humanoid? They were bisymmetrical, anyway, highly intelligent, and by all accounts no worse than indifferent to the interests of other species. So beautiful and graceful was their slender physicality, so mellifluous their speech, that even though they were quite alien the idea of living among them held no fear for Jonos. Anything, he knew, would be a step up from Earth. Lost on Paradise by Alan Dean Foster: $19.99 New York Times bestselling author Alan Dean Foster, master of both action and emotion, reveals a world where everything is perfect, but nothing is as it seems…

item.title: AI will eat a fifth of tech budgets in 2027, but don't expect it to pay for itself
item.description: More than half of CIOs are likely to miss their AI-related ROI targets next year, according to Forrester. The analyst firm's State Of AI Survey 2026 found that 45 percent of AI decision-makers need positive ROI within a year to consider their investments successful. Some tech leaders will get better at tying AI spend to planned returns. However, Forrester expects success to be confined to isolated use cases rather than whole programs, which won't be enough. “As with prior emerging technologies, organizational structures, processes, and ways of working need to change to drive measurable, firmwide results with AI,” the report says. Only 22 percent of AI decision-makers report a positive AI impact on EBITDA (earnings before income tax, depreciation and amortization) over the past 12 months. “This mismatch between the investment into technology adoption and organizational change will delay the realization of heightened ROI targets,” the report adds. The money will keep flowing through IT budgets regardless. In its Technology & Security Predictions, Forrester claimed AI will account for 20 percent of all business technology spend next year. Sharyn Leaver, chief research officer at Forrester, said that will increase the pressure on leaders to prove AI's value while keeping costs, infrastructure, and risk under control. “At the same time, emerging technologies, geopolitical pressures, and the growing use of AI across technology operations will introduce new complexities and potential points of failure,” she said. While tech teams struggle to get returns from growing AI spending, they will try to get more bang for their buck by investing in open-weight GenAI models, which can approach similar performance to the leading proprietary systems, at a fraction of the cost. Open-weight models will represent half of AI tokens but only five percent of enterprise spend, Forrester predicts. “Open-weight models such as Gemma, Llama, or Qwen are good enough for the enterprise workloads that generate the most token volume, such as document processing, customer support conversations, internal knowledge search, and the routine substeps inside agentic workflows,” Forrester said. Frontier models, including Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, and Google's Gemini 4 Argon, will be reserved for “the few deep knowledge and critical task automations where errors are expensive, but the token count will tip toward open weight”, Forrester said.

item.title: Signal bug could keep your mic - and camera - on after hangup
item.description: Make sure you don’t say anything mean or secret after hanging up a call on Signal, as a bug in the encrypted messaging app’s calling library could prevent a call from ending properly, potentially leaving audio and possibly video active. The vulnerability, CVE-2026-113380 , was published by MITRE on Tuesday and given a CVSS score of 9.3, marking it as a critical issue in Signal’s open-source RingRTC library in every single version before 2.72.0. That update was pushed out last month, but the vulnerability wasn’t made public until now. RingRTC is Signal’s own calling library built on top of WebRTC , a technology introduced in 2011 that has since become widely used for voice and video communication over the internet. RingRTC provides Signal-specific calling functionality using WebRTC, which already encrypts media traffic, but that isn't stopping RingRTC from failing to hang up calls in certain conditions, according to the CVE report. What’s happening is, in essence, a denial-of-service attack on RingRTC’s finite state machine (FSM) event queue, which handles events involved in managing calls. If one of the people on the call saturates the FSM queue with requests, it can become overwhelmed and fail to process a hangup request, preventing the call from terminating properly. The vulnerability is classified as CWE-754 , or improper checking for unusual or exceptional conditions, according to a report posted to GitHub. A conceptual proof of concept is available in the GitHub report linked above, using a Python script to simulate how flooding an event queue can prevent a hangup request from being processed. Were a malicious actor to exploit this, the person on the other end may think the call has been terminated, but either or both of their video and audio channels could still be open. The attack complexity is considered low according to the CVE, and while CISA’s known exploited vulnerabilities catalog doesn’t indicate this has been spotted in the wild, Signal users ought to ensure they’ve updated their apps - mobile and desktop - to the latest versions to ensure they don’t end up being caught on a hot mic without any notice. Comparing RingRTC 2.72.0 to the previous version indicates that Signal's fix allows the call's finite state machine (FSM) to detect termination requests independently of the event queue, while adding a timeout to prevent stalled processing from indefinitely blocking a hangup. It's not entirely clear from Signal's release notes when the fixed version of RingRTC reached the Android, iOS, and desktop versions of its apps. Signal Desktop's release history indicates that RingRTC 2.72.0 was incorporated in September, but the precise rollout dates across all platforms remain unclear. We’ve reached out to Signal to learn more, but haven’t heard back. In the meantime, best to update your installation to be sure you’re not still vulnerable. That, and watch what you say after hanging up a call. ®

item.title: 5 Nollywood Movies to Watch on Streaming Platforms Before October Ends
item.description: Toyin Abraham’s directorial comedy drama Oversabi Aunty is now streaming on Netflix and Kava. Your next movie night could take you from a hilarious Nollywood comedy to a fantasy world full of adventure, or straight into a crime story that keeps you guessing. With several Nollywood films and series now available to stream, there’s plenty to add to your watchlist before October wraps up. Whether you’re in the mood for a box-office hit you missed at the cinema or a moving coming-of-age story, these are the titles worth making time for. Oversabi Aunty (Streaming on Kava TV and Netflix) Toyin Abraham ’s record-breaking directorial debut follows Toun, a self-righteous church usher whose overzealous obsession with fixing everyone else’s morals turns her home and family life into a chaotic battlefield. Her relentless meddling reaches its breaking point during a disastrous family introduction, forcing her to confront the emotional fallout and damage she has caused her loved ones. Directed, written, and produced by Toyin Abraham alongside FilmOne Studios, the witty dramedy features an ensemble cast including Toyin Abraham, Mike Ezuruonye , Jemima Osunde , Tana Adelana , Efe Irele , Enioluwa Adeoluwa , and Queen Nwokoye . Colours of Fire (Streaming on Netflix) Niyi Akinmolayan ’s epic fantasy film takes viewers into an ancient world where the fabric-weaving Blue Tribe and the mysterious Red Tribe maintain a bitter, generational conflict. When a warrior named Akinbode is sent to eliminate a beast terrorising his people, his unexpected encounter with Moremi—the daughter of the Red Tribe’s queen—ignites a forbidden romance that challenges inherited stories and threatens to unravel their entire society. Directed and written by Niyi Akinmolayan, with production credits from Anthill Studios, FilmOne Studios, and Imuetinyan Productions, the visually rich film stars Uzor Arukwe , Osas Ighodaro , Mercy Aigbe , Gabriel Afolayan , Femi Branch , and Ibrahim Chatta . Ordinary People (Streaming on Netflix) Moses Inwang ’s crime thriller series dives deep into the gritty, interconnected lives of characters navigating power, ambition, and survival across the streets of Lagos and beyond. The story exposes how everyday decisions spiral into high-stakes consequences when ordinary individuals find themselves caught in webbed conflicts and dangerous secrets. Created, directed, and written by Moses Inwang, the eight-episode production features a powerhouse cast starring Ramsey Nouah , Adunni Ade , Chidi Mokeme , Sharon Ooja , Michelle Dede , Shawn Faqua , Lasisi Elenu , Uche Montana , and Jackie Appiah . Where Is Mr Right? (Streaming on Prime Video) Tunde Olaoye ’s romantic drama follows Bunmi, an event planner facing immense societal and familial pressure to get married before crossing an arbitrary age milestone. Her determined quest to locate an ideal partner spirals into a series of comedic missteps, unexpected heartbreaks, and lessons on patience and self-discovery. Directed

item.title: NASA to Conduct NCAA Flyover, Engage Fans at University of Alabama
item.description: NASA’s Freedom 250 F-5 team, including NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, performs a flyover during the national anthem at an NFL game between the Cleveland Browns and the Carolina Panthers at Huntington Bank Field, Sept. 27, 2026, in Cleveland. NASA/Jordan Cochran As part of the agency’s Inspiration Tour, NASA will conduct a flyover at the University of Alabama vs. Texas A&M football game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, on Saturday, Oct. 24. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will pilot one of three F-5 fighter jets during the flyover, highlighting NASA’s contributions to aeronautics and the agency’s continued commitment to advancing aviation technologies. Ahead of the game, members of the news media are invited to visit the NASA Experience Zone on Champions Lane, where Isaacman will participate in a media opportunity at 11 a.m. CDT. Media interested in attending should confirm their attendance by 12 p.m. Friday, Oct. 23, with Lance D. Davis at lance.d.davis@nasa.gov to receive additional details and instructions. Supported by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the NASA Experience Zone will be open to the public from 10:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. CDT, with no game ticket required. The experience will give visitors an opportunity to meet NASA team members and learn more about the people and technologies advancing the agency’s missions in aeronautics and space exploration. Attendees can engage with NASA team members and explore exhibits highlighting the agency’s Artemis campaign and efforts to return astronauts to the Moon, including: An inflatable SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. Displays featuring the Starship and Blue Moon human landing systems. Information about NASA internship opportunities. Photo opportunities featuring NASA exhibits and displays. With stops across the nation, NASA’s Inspiration Tour convenes academic, industry, and public sector stakeholders to connect the agency with the people, technologies, and organizations that drive American leadership in space. The tour will culminate in MAX POWER, a public exposition of American air and space innovation, Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Held in honor of America’s historic 250th anniversary, the multi-day, family-friendly event will showcase the next-generation aircraft, spacecraft, autonomous vehicles, and technologies that will help define the future of transportation in air and space. For more information about MAX POWER and the agency’s missions, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/maxpower -end- Lance D. item.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good

item.title: Tracks Along the Longest Drive on Another World

The image was acquired with its Left Navigation Camera on Oct. 11, 2026 (Sol 2006) at a local mean solar time of 14:40:39. NASA/JPL-Caltech Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory Oct. 12, 2026 Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. Its engineering twin here on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records celebrating the achievement. Two months ago, on Sol 1947, the odometer sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive using Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav). However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time executing short drives to perform rock abrasions and proximity science on ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record. On its way to the drive record, Perseverance has navigated challenging terrain while also pioneering new ways to drive across the Martian surface. Perseverance’s various encounters with dense boulder fields and steep slopes have pushed the team to re-evaluate driving guidelines so the rover is better prepared to handle tough terrain. After running thousands of simulations, the team raised the rover’s tilt limit to 24 degrees and reduced the clearance required under the rover’s belly pan to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches). The team also updated the rover’s braking software to avoid rock hazards, nearly doubled steer motor current limits, updated flight software with “dynamic slip tables” to model expected slip, and used cross-slope driving to better anchor wheels on exposed bedrock. One of the most exciting updates the team has made is an autonomous drive capability called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). item.content:encoded: Explore This Section Perseverance Home Mission Overview Rover Components Mars Rock Samples Where is Perseverance? Ingenuity Mars Helicopter Mission Updates Science Overview Objectives Instruments Highlights Exploration Goals News and Features Multimedia Perseverance Raw Images Images Videos Audio More Resources Mars Missions Mars Perseverance Rover Mars Curiosity Rover Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Odyssey More Mars Missions Mars Home This image, taken by Perseverance on Mars, shows wheel tracks from the drive that broke the record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. The image was acquired with its Left Navigation Camera on Oct. 11, 2026 (Sol 2006) at a local mean solar time of 14:40:39. NASA/JPL-Caltech Written by Vandi Verma, Chief Engineer for Robotic Operations at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory Oct. 12, 2026 Since the last blog update, Perseverance has achieved a major milestone on Mars. On Sol 2006 (Oct. 11, 2026), its odometer reached 45.22 kilometers (28.10 miles), setting a new record for the farthest distance driven on another celestial body. Its engineering twin here on Earth even received a plaque from Guinness World Records celebrating the achievement. Two months ago, on Sol 1947, the odometer sat about 200 meters away from the milestone, a distance easily achievable with a single drive using Autonomous Navigation (AutoNav). However, the rover found itself in a very scientifically interesting area and spent time executing short drives to perform rock abrasions and proximity science on ancient rock outcrops. When Perseverance was finally ready to move on to a new site, it sailed past the record. On its way to the drive record, Perseverance has navigated challenging terrain while also pioneering new ways to drive across the Martian surface. Perseverance’s various encounters with dense boulder fields and steep slopes have pushed the team to re-evaluate driving guidelines so the rover is better prepared to handle tough terrain. After running thousands of simulations, the team raised the rover’s tilt limit to 24 degrees and reduced the clearance required under the rover’s belly pan to 20 centimeters (about 7.9 inches). The team also updated the rover’s braking software to avoid rock hazards, nearly doubled steer motor current limits, updated flight software with “dynamic slip tables” to model expected slip, and used cross-slope driving to better anchor wheels on exposed bedrock. One of the most exciting updates the team has made is an autonomous drive capability called onboard Global Localization (GBLC). GBLC repurposes the high-speed commercial processor inside the Ingenuity Helicopter Base Station to compare ground and orbital imagery to autonomously locate the rover in global coordinates at the end of a drive (as though we had GPS on a world without it), enabling Perseverance to drive longer distances without human intervention. Unlike Perseverance’s main flight computer, this coprocessor is not hardened against the punishing radiation environment of the Martian surface, where a thin atmosphere and the lack of a global magnetosphere leave little shielding. This radiation can induce “transient bit flips” in memory the software needs to function, and the team developed an effective software-based approach to radiation hardening. Looking forward to the greater demands of longer drives and to planning more activity with fewer resources, the team is also exploring the use of generative SI to help efficiently propose solutions to steer AutoNav along the many legs of a strategic path. The team is using hard-won lessons from 45 kilometers (more than 28 miles) of driving to reinvent how the rover drives across the Martian surface. As Perseverance climbs higher along the crater rim, the next leap in autonomous exploration on Mars is just getting started. Want to read more posts from the Perseverance team? item.title: OpenBSD 8.0 beefs up virtual machines and gets a taste of Wine
item.description: OpenBSD 8.0 brings bigger virtual machines, graphics improvements, and another helping of AI mockery. The round version number doesn't signal a radical break with its predecessors. OpenBSD 8.0 is the 61st release of the project. Developer Bryan Steele posted a highlights rundown on Mastodon. Wireless improvements include updates to the qwx driver for Qualcomm Wi-Fi 6 hardware. Its VMM/VMD hypervisor now supports multiprocessor VMs with up to 64 virtual CPUs in each guest. The kernel virtual memory address space on x86-64 is now 512 GB, up from 4 GB, allowing for GPUs with large amounts of VRAM. On Arm64 machines, OpenBSD supports hibernation, and on both x86-64 and Arm64 it can use CPU AES instructions for faster encrypted swap. Component upgrades include OpenSSH 10.6 and LibreSSL 4.4.0, and the DRM graphics driver stack from Linux 6.18. The default C compiler is Clang/LLVM 22, including for the SPARC64 edition – but at the cost of dropping support for the Loongson architecture. The list of errata is short, with just four fixes – but then, version 8.0 is very new. Just days before this release, there was a high-profile OpenBSD issue: Calif's "Big Fish" research describes a decades-old shared-memory bug chained with a separate kernel flaw to gain local root access. Both were fixed in OpenBSD 7.9 , through errata 026 and 018 respectively. Project leader Theo de Raadt forked OpenBSD from NetBSD 1.0 in 1995, and the first release of the new OS was OpenBSD 1.2 in July 1996 – so version 8.0 is as close as the project will get to a 30th anniversary release. According to Calif's proof-of-concept code on GitHub , the bug was in the original code that both OpenBSD and NetBSD inherited from the original BSD codebase – which is how come there's a 37-year-old bug in a 30-year-old project. A HackerNews comment says: "Interestingly, looks like this was accidentally fixed in NetBSD during a rewrite of that code in August of 1999." The project has not updated its infamous slogan. The homepage still proclaims: "Only two remote holes in the default install, in a heck of a long time!" As we noted in May when OpenBSD 7.9 appeared , the project rejects code generated by LLMs, although on the basis of licensing concerns rather than its cousin NetBSD's explicit anti-AI stance . As we reported recently , this strict anti-AI stance seems to be serving NetBSD well. OpenBSD is also an anti-AI project, and for this release, the website goes out of its way to make that very clear. OpenBSD's mascot is a pufferfish, and in the banner artwork for the new release, "Puffy" has an extra eye – and the signpost in the image's background also has malformed text, a hallmark of early image-generation bots. The eyes are also constantly blinking – one at a time – to emphasize that this is a reference to Blinky the mutant fish from The Simpsons. In case you missed The Simpsons reference, the version 8.0 release theme song makes it even more explicit: it's titled "The Simps on AI." The lyri
item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: OpenBSD 8.0 brings bigger virtual machines, graphics improvements, and another helping of AI mockery. The round version number doesn't signal a radical break with its predecessors. OpenBSD 8.0 is the 61st release of the project. Developer Bryan Steele posted a highlights rundown on Mastodon. Wireless improvements include updates to the qwx driver for Qualcomm Wi-Fi 6 hardware. Its VMM/VMD hypervisor now supports multiprocessor VMs with up to 64 virtual CPUs in each guest. The kernel virtual memory address space on x86-64 is now 512 GB, up from 4 GB, allowing for GPUs with large amounts of VRAM. On Arm64 machines, OpenBSD supports hibernation, and on both x86-64 and Arm64 it can use CPU AES instructions for faster encrypted swap. Component upgrades include OpenSSH 10.6 and LibreSSL 4.4.0, and the DRM graphics driver stack from Linux 6.18. The default C compiler is Clang/LLVM 22, including for the SPARC64 edition – but at the cost of dropping support for the Loongson architecture. The list of errata is short, with just four fixes – but then, version 8.0 is very new. Just days before this release, there was a high-profile OpenBSD issue: Calif's "Big Fish" research describes a decades-old shared-memory bug chained with a separate kernel flaw to gain local root access. Both were fixed in OpenBSD 7.9 , through errata 026 and 018 respectively. Project leader Theo de Raadt forked OpenBSD from NetBSD 1.0 in 1995, and the first release of the new OS was OpenBSD 1.2 in July 1996 – so version 8.0 is as close as the project will get to a 30th anniversary release. According to Calif's proof-of-concept code on GitHub , the bug was in the original code that both OpenBSD and NetBSD inherited from the original BSD codebase – which is how come there's a 37-year-old bug in a 30-year-old project. A HackerNews comment says: "Interestingly, looks like this was accidentally fixed in NetBSD during a rewrite of that code in August of 1999." The project has not updated its infamous slogan. The homepage still proclaims: "Only two remote holes in the default install, in a heck of a long time!" As we noted in May when OpenBSD 7.9 appeared , the project rejects code generated by LLMs, although on the basis of licensing concerns rather than its cousin NetBSD's explicit anti-AI stance . As we reported recently , this strict anti-AI stance seems to be serving NetBSD well. OpenBSD is also an anti-AI project, and for this release, the website goes out of its way to make that very clear. OpenBSD's mascot is a pufferfish, and in the banner artwork for the new release, "Puffy" has an extra eye – and the signpost in the image's background also has malformed text, a hallmark of early image-generation bots. The eyes are also constantly blinking – one at a time – to emphasize that this is a reference to Blinky the mutant fish from The Simpsons. In case you missed The Simpsons reference, the version 8.0 release theme song makes it even more explicit: it's titled "The Simps on AI." The lyrics and the vocals parody both Simpsons characters and AI users. Our favorite line sounds like Grampa Simpson, and says: Back in my day we didn't have artificial intelligence, we had real stupidity – and we liked it. We've seen negative reactions online, but then we often find that some people lack much of a sense of humor. For our part, we really enjoyed seeing the OpenBSD team having such fun. We reckon it will appeal to many Butlerian Jihadi types. It certainly did to The Reg FOSS desk. A little Wine with your pufferfish A couple of days before the 8.0 release came an unexpected announcement on the openbsd-ports mailing list: a proposed port of Wine for OpenBSD . This is a new version of the Wine 11 runtime that allows Windows binaries to launch and run on OpenBSD. This is a 64-bit version of Wine for OpenBSD on x86-64, and for now, this means it can only run 64-bit Windows code. (For the technical nitty-gritty: Wine needs to manipulate the CPU's GS register. Windows on x86-64 uses the GS segment base to locate the Thread Environment Block (TEB), as the late great Geoff Chappell explained . This is a very longstanding Windows data structure, going all the way back through Windows 95 to OS/2 . The port was particularly tricky because OpenBSD doesn't allow programs to alter that, so the port is emulating instructions that use the %gs segment override. The snags are that this means 32-bit code doesn't work, and secondly, because this is unnecessary on Linux, the code is unlikely to be merged back into upstream Wine.) If you want to see it working, there are a few screenshot galleries on Reddit's openbsd_gaming group, showing a number of recent major titles running: Some samples from WIP wine port , more wine-on-OpenBSD screenshots , and even more wine-on-OpenBSD proof . The port comes hedged with caveats, notable among them that Wine does not do any kind of sandboxing, so using it potentially opens up OpenBSD to Windows malware. However, for some users, this could be a very useful addition. OpenBSD is the simplest and cleanest member of the BSD family, indeed, of the FOSS Unix family. Part of this is because entire subsystems are missing that the other BSDs provide. Bluetooth connections to Apple's wireless keyboards and pointing devices aren't supported. There's no logical volume management – which would massively help with OpenBSD's complex disk partitioning. There's no journaling filesystem either (although a port of the new Gefs is in progress ). While small and clean, its priorities favor security and simplicity, though performance will depend on the hardware and workload. Importantly – since you probably will need to ask for help – the OpenBSD community does not have a reputation for friendliness. Saying that, it is quite a lot easier to get OpenBSD installed and running, complete with its 25-year-old version 2.2.5 of the Fvwm window manager , than either NetBSD or FreeBSD. If you're looking for an AI-free, and indeed systemd-free, path away from Linux, OpenBSD 8.0 is very definitely worth a try. ®

item.title: 3 Toyin Abraham-Inspired Owambe Looks for Your Next Saturday Party
item.description: Three traditional Owambe style moments from Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi featuring velvet, damask, and aso-oke. When Nollywood actor and filmmaker Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi is not busy preparing for her highly anticipated festive cinematic release, Bestie , or writing, producing, and starring in box-office hits like Fate of Alakada , Ijakumo : The Born Again Stripper , and The Ghost and the Tout , she is usually showing us how to nail weekend celebrations. As one of the most prominent faces in Nigerian cinema, her personal style outside the cinema hall has become a major source of fashion inspiration, especially when it comes to pulling off unforgettable Owambe looks. Styling traditional wear for a Saturday party comes down to knowing how to mix colours, textures, and rich fabrics without losing that classic touch. Wearing black and silver to a Nigerian party is all about balance. While dark tones are traditionally avoided for daytime celebrations, pairing a deep black velvet blouse with a metallic silver scalloped-lace skirt completely changes the mood. Draping a silver-grey paisley ipele over the shoulder alongside a matching pleated geleadds instant brightness, while traditional coral beads anchor the entire outfit. Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi showing how to wear black and silver to a Nigerian party. Photo Credit: Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi/Instagram For anyone leaning towards rich jewel tones, crimson velvet offers an instant sense of luxury. Tailoring a solid burgundy velvet gown into a clean, floor-length silhouette provides a sleek base, but adding a patterned teal and magenta damask ipele across one shoulder breaks up the solid fabric. Crowning the look with a structured fan gele in the same damask print brings the entire outfit together. Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi styling crimson velvet and patterned damask for traditional Owambe inspiration. Photo Credit: Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi/Instagram Bright colours always command attention in party halls, and mustard yellow offers a warmer, sophisticated take on sunshine yellow. Tailoring the fabric into a traditional buba and iro set with horizontal black lace bands and tassel-fringe details along the wrapper adds movement and texture. Matching the ensemble with a rounded mustard gele and subtle gold jewellery keeps the palette grounded while letting the traditional silhouette shine. Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi wearing a mustard yellow buba and iro with black lace fringe details for party inspiration. Photo Credit: Toyin Abraham Ajeyemi/Instagram The post 3 Toyin Abraham-Inspired Owambe Looks for Your Next Saturday Party appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: PHP devs publish critical bug fix as site owners warned: Pull 'em offline if you're unpatched
item.description: PHP developers have released emergency updates for two critical vulnerabilities after cybersecurity authorities warned organizations to patch immediately or consider taking exposed applications offline. PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. The project's developers urged users to update immediately . All PHP installations serving web requests are potentially affected, including deployments using PHP-FPM, Apache's mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, the developers said. "We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs." Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at watchTowr, said: "As expected, watchTowr Intel is already observing in-the-wild exploitation of the latest PHP vulnerabilities, with a variety of vibecoded PoCs already hitting our sensors featuring a variety of 'php2shell' User-Agents. Whilst nobody has been successful to date, we don't expect that will last long." "Where immediate patching is not feasible, organizations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available," CERT-EU said in an advisory issued ahead of the patches. The body lists both vulnerabilities with CVSS scores of 9.2. Finnish government services and websites belonging to the Dutch parliament, cybersecurity authorities, and data protection regulator were taken offline as a precaution. Privacy campaign group noyb also temporarily withdrew its website. PHP "powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," infosec vendor Huntress noted . That makes identifying exposed installations a substantial job. "The number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast," said John Hammond, Huntress's senior principal security researcher. ®

item.title: Science on the Space Station with NASA Astronaut Jessica Watkins
item.description: NASA/Anil Menon NASA astronaut and Expedition 75 flight engineer Jessica Watkins works inside the Kibo laboratory module’s Life Science Glovebox on Oct. 9, 2026, safely mixing living cell samples with a bioink and then filling a special cartridge with the cell‑ink mixture. The advanced research operations were part of the InSPA‑Auxilium Bioprinter‑Cell Printing investigation, which explores 3D bioprinting cartilage tissue in microgravity of higher quality than that produced on Earth. Results may advance the ability to biomanufacture cartilage, benefiting patients on Earth and crew members on long‑duration space missions. Image credit: NASA/Anil Menon

item.title: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
item.description: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well? In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says. That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew? Continue reading...

item.title: Jensen Huang sends in the robot ducks to sell Nvidia's AI-everywhere vision
item.description: Cute robots stole the show at Nvidia's GTC keynote in Berlin, where Jensen Huang pitched a future powered by AI agents – and, naturally, plenty of his company's hardware. The Nvidia chief remained his usual ebullient self despite environmental protesters interrupting his presentation at Berlin's tent-shaped Tempodrom. "Why don't you clean up your act?" they demanded, holding up banners that partially obscured the presentation screen behind Huang. "All important issues, but let me get through my keynote," he joked, adding: "I'll talk to you guys later," as security swiftly removed them. Huang was discussing Vera Rubin systems before unveiling DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI infrastructure . DSX POD combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks using Nvidia's Spectrum-X networking. Partners will cable, integrate, and test the systems in modular containers before delivery, with availability expected in early 2027. Nvidia claims deployment could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site. That excludes the not insignificant matter of getting power, connectivity, and other site infrastructure ready first. He was keen to add that Vera Rubin systems are designed for closed-loop liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45°C, while outdoor dry coolers release heat into the air without needing to evaporate water. "At 2 gigawatts, DSX can save 54 million litres of water a day," Huang claimed, perhaps thinking of those environmental protesters. The Microducks from Pollen Robotics are small, two-legged robots with cameras for faces. Huang interacted with them on stage, getting them to lie down and roll over by voice command, and the little robots all beeped back at him in response. The robo ducks demonstrated a workflow in which AI was trained in the cloud, evaluated on an Nvidia RTX Spark PC, then deployed on the robots. item.content:encoded: Cute robots stole the show at Nvidia's GTC keynote in Berlin, where Jensen Huang pitched a future powered by AI agents – and, naturally, plenty of his company's hardware. The Nvidia chief remained his usual ebullient self despite environmental protesters interrupting his presentation at Berlin's tent-shaped Tempodrom. "Why don't you clean up your act?" they demanded, holding up banners that partially obscured the presentation screen behind Huang. "All important issues, but let me get through my keynote," he joked, adding: "I'll talk to you guys later," as security swiftly removed them. Huang was discussing Vera Rubin systems before unveiling DSX POD, a reference design for factory-built, containerized AI infrastructure . DSX POD combines seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin compute racks using Nvidia's Spectrum-X networking. Partners will cable, integrate, and test the systems in modular containers before delivery, with availability expected in early 2027. Nvidia claims deployment could shrink from six months to as little as 14 days at a prepared site. That excludes the not insignificant matter of getting power, connectivity, and other site infrastructure ready first. He was keen to add that Vera Rubin systems are designed for closed-loop liquid cooling with coolant temperatures up to 45°C, while outdoor dry coolers release heat into the air without needing to evaporate water. "At 2 gigawatts, DSX can save 54 million litres of water a day," Huang claimed, perhaps thinking of those environmental protesters. Yet much of the leather-jacketed leader's attention was focused on physical AI: robots, autonomous vehicles, and other machinery Nvidia hopes to supply with its hardware and software. The Microducks from Pollen Robotics are small, two-legged robots with cameras for faces. Huang interacted with them on stage, getting them to lie down and roll over by voice command, and the little robots all beeped back at him in response. The robo ducks demonstrated a workflow in which AI was trained in the cloud, evaluated on an Nvidia RTX Spark PC, then deployed on the robots. Huang also unveiled Agile ONE SN, a humanoid robot reference platform from German robotics startup Agile Robots, based on Nvidia's Isaac GR00T technology and a Jetson Thor compute module. Scheduled for early 2027, the platform is intended to give robotics researchers and developers a ready-made system for developing and testing capabilities. "This is going to be the next major industry, the next great industry," Huang claimed. Beyond robots, Nvidia is pushing its AI hardware and software into cars and telecoms networks. Huang boasted that Nvidia's Hyperion car system is being adopted by more vendors, saying: "We turned this into an industry standard, and now it's being designed into one car fleet after another." Europe's telecoms operators are also deploying Nvidia-powered computing in their networks to deliver advanced services using AI-RAN, according to Huang. "After working on this for nearly eight years, Nvidia made the first commercial phone call on the T-Mobile network with Nokia, and so now CUDA makes phone calls," he said. Far from slowing down the progression of AI, it seems Nvidia is determined to push its technology into every corner of the world. "Everyone will become an AI company," Huang claimed. He also took care to praise Europe and its technology efforts while he was in Berlin. "As expected, Jensen positioned Nvidia as a strong supporter of – and enabler for – Europe's sovereign tech ambitions. Nvidia has invested almost $10 billion into Europe in the past year, including 14 investments into European startups during Jensen's current trip," said Forrester principal analyst Paul Miller. But Miller pointed out that Nvidia itself is not European. "Anything with critical ongoing dependencies on Nvidia (or any other non-European firm) is unlikely to meet the purest definitions of European tech sovereignty," he added. Huang closed with a CGI video of robots performing a Eurovision-style song recapping his keynote. Yes, it was as bad as you imagine. ®

item.title: “I Never Really Thought of Insects as Beautiful Creatures” – Dara Ojo on Becoming a Macro Photographer
item.description: Nigerian Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Dara Ojo was stuck at home in China, like everyone else in the world. He had recently picked up photography, and that allowed him to explore and pay close attention to his immediate surroundings. One day, he started paying closer attention to the tiny creatures around him and was amazed by what he was seeing. There were colours, patterns, behaviours and details that he had never noticed before. It felt like discovering an entirely different world that had been right in front of me all along. Dara self-taught himself macro photography, and the seemingly small curiosity during the pandemic has grown into a journey of documenting biodiversity across Nigeria, Canada, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador and beyond. His work has travelled globally and has been featured in major international publications. Dara has photographed over 40 types of spiders, 50 species of moths, 30 species of butterflies, more than 20 dragonflies, and at least 70 damselflies. There are many photographers in Nigeria, but seeing that macro photography is not often explored by Nigerians, we sat down for a brief conversation with Dara, where he shared what inspired his form of photography, what documenting biodiversity in different environments has taught him about nature and his forthcoming first photography book, Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. Leafhopper infected by Metarhizium Fungus. Photo by Dara Ojo. Hey Dara, how are you feeling? I feel good. I feel blessed. Thank you for having me. What do you think inspired or attracted you to macro photography? Growing up in Nigeria, I never really thought of insects as something beautiful or worth photographing. Like many people, I saw them as creatures you either avoided or tried to get rid of. But once I started looking at them through my camera, my perspective completely changed. What fascinated me most wasn’t just how they looked, but how they lived. I started asking questions. Why does this spider behave this way? How does that tiny insect survive? What role does it play in nature? The more I discovered, the more curious I became. Six years later, that curiosity has taken me from photographing tiny creatures around my neighbourhood in China to exploring rainforests and other ecosystems across different continents. And the interesting thing is that I still experience that same excitement whenever I discover something new. I don’t think that feeling will ever go away. Bumblebee by macro photographer, Dara Ojo.
